prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I opened with DMFT (B020), and I still think it is a first-rate achievement. Reading the other seven ballots, though, I do not see colleagues who share that ranking, and I should not treat my own methods background as scientific merit. Optical lattice clocks (B018) are the strongest case on the table once the evidence is read across ballots. Four members place it first. The discovery is a specific, measurable instrument advance rather than a field label: the magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil limits and brings fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18, with independent confirmation by many national and university laboratories and direct consequences for the SI second, tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. The attribution is unusually clean, Katori for the concept and first demonstrations and Ye for taking the clock to record accuracy and many-body-limited regimes, and it fits a two-person prize without the allocation fights that afflict the other candidates. I also value that this is quantum mechanics put to work in a precision measurement, in the spirit of 'continually offers new surprises' that I said when announcing the 2025 prize as Chair, and the maturity is plainly timely rather than premature.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the redefinition of the second is still pending, so some may argue for waiting for that milestone, and that frequency-comb and ion-clock contributors (Hall and Hansch were recognised in 2005, Wineland in 2012) lie close by, so the prize could be read as an incremental extension of a recognised metrology lineage. There is also a risk that a clean attribution is bought by omitting real contributors to the strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks. Finally, I rank B018 outside my own expertise in electronic structure, so I defer to Kroll, Lindroth and Danielsson on the technical claims about systematic uncertainties and lattice-clock physics.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks optical lattice clocks first because the instrument rests on a clear conceptual idea (Katori's magic wavelength), reaches 1e-18, and has stable, timely recognition, and he ranks twistronics (B044) second.
responses.response: I agree with the first half and have moved to it. The point that the instrument rests on a clear conceptual idea is what persuades me, because it gives a precise answer to the attribution question that I could not resolve for DMFT. On B044 I partly part ways with him: I also ranked it highly, but I would not put it ahead of a settled discovery while the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated insulators are still unresolved, and the experimental credit (Cao and other groups) is contested. His own ballot concedes that Cao is missing from the credit.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube neutrino astronomy first as a new messenger measured in nature, with Halzen as the intellectual driver and Karle central to construction, and prefers a two-person prize without Yoshida.
responses.response: I take seriously that a new observational window is the kind of discovery the prize was created for, and the diffuse flux is secure. My reservation is attribution. In a collaboration of several hundred, a two-person credit for Halzen and Karle is a representative choice rather than a decisive one, and the blazar and Galactic-plane associations are still maturing. Mehlig says outright that he cannot tell who played the decisive role in the analyses, and I share that doubt. For me that makes B007 a close second to the clocks rather than the lead.

responses.point: Johansson ranks the Cirac-Zoller trapped-ion and cold-atom proposals first as the blueprint that made quantum computation and simulation concrete, with theory-only credit justified because the experimental ion-gate side was recognised in 2012.
responses.response: The originality is not in doubt, and the pair is a clean credit. My serious qualification is that a theory-only prize for proposals leans on experimental realisations that are largely credited elsewhere, as Lindroth also notes, and a 2012 prize was already given for the experimental half. I also note that the same two names (with Bloch and Greiner) appear in B015, so recognising them under B032 would draw on overlapping material. Compared with lattice clocks, where the proposal and the decisive demonstration share two names, the case for B032 is less self-contained, though I would keep it on the table if the committee prefers a theory prize.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics first as a general, conceptually clean framework confirmed in colloids, single-molecule experiments and quantum devices, with Evans, Jarzynski and Seifert as three decisive steps and Crooks as the awkward omission.
responses.response: I find the framework conceptually elegant and agree that experiments from optical tweezers to RNA unfolding support it, so I do not dispute the physics. My difficulty is that the credited set has four names for a three-person limit, and by his own account the omission of Crooks is awkward, so the allocation is no cleaner than for topological insulators. I would also ask whether the prize-level discovery is a single result with a measurable consequence, or a family of relations. I would want to hear him argue which of the three steps carries the citation, since no other member ranked B002.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first and IceCube second, notes that Mele's role matters as much as Kane's in B034, and recognises that the circuit-QED area is close to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I agree on B018 and on her observation that a three-person topological configuration inevitably leaves out deserving contributors; Mele should not be dropped in favour of Hasan, and I would write B034 as Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as I did in my own ballot. Her point about the proximity of circuit QED to the 2025 prize is, as the Chair of that cycle, one I recognise: B008 is a different discovery, but the committee cannot ignore the perception of a second prize in the same area so soon.

uncertainties: Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay recognition of optical lattice clocks.

Whether Walter Metzner and the early contributors to the infinite-dimension limit (relevant to B020, my opening first choice) can be accommodated within a three-person DMFT configuration, so B020 stays an alternative rather than my lead.
Whether the other contributors to strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks create an attribution problem that the two-name credit hides.
How to rank the late-stage twistronics case (B044) against settled discoveries while the origin of the superconductivity is unresolved.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional conflict with the shortlisted candidates is apparent from my provided profile. I should disclose that my own research field (electronic-structure theory, DFT and DFT+DMFT, magnetism) is close to B020, B003, B034 and B044, which is a methodological bias rather than a recusal issue, and that my opening first choice, B020, came from that background.
